opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was honestly one of the hardest decisions I've had to make, because both paths were really attractive in different ways.

On the faculty side, the appeal is obvious. You get a lot of intellectual freedom, you get to work with students and watch them grow, and you can pursue long-horizon questions without having to justify them against a product roadmap. For someone who came up through academia, that's kind of the default dream, and I think a part of me always assumed that's where I'd end up.

But when I thought about it more concretely, I kept coming back to one question: where is the bottleneck in robotics right now? For a long time, I think the bottleneck was ideas. Better algorithms, better formulations, better ways of thinking about control and learning. Academia is fantastic for that. But my sense is that, at least for the kind of general-purpose robot learning I care about, a big part of the bottleneck has shifted toward scale. It's about data collection across many robots and many tasks, serious compute, solid engineering infrastructure, and a team that can iterate really fast together. Those are things that are very hard to assemble in a single university lab, no matter how talented the students are.

So in a way, the choice became less "industry versus academia" and more "which environment lets me actually test the ideas I believe in." If you think foundation models for robotics are a real direction, you kind of have to be somewhere that can build them at a meaningful scale. Otherwise you're always extrapolating from small experiments and hoping the trend holds.

The people mattered a lot too. Physical Intelligence brought together researchers I really respected, people whose work I'd been reading and learning from for years. Being in the same room with them, arguing about what matters, felt like a rare opportunity, and it's the kind of thing that might not be available again in the same form a few years later. Faculty positions, by contrast, are something you can still pursue later in your career. The window for being part of something like this at an early stage felt much narrower.

That said, I don't see it as a permanent goodbye to academia. A lot of what I loved about academic research, the openness, publishing, mentoring, thinking carefully about fundamental questions, I think you can carry some of that spirit into a place like this. And maybe at some point I'll go back with a much better sense of what actually works at scale, which I think would make me a better advisor anyway.

So the short version is: I asked myself where I could learn the most and where I could have the most direct impact on the problem I care about over the next few years, and the answer pointed pretty clearly to Physical Intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a clean comparison, because the two paths optimize for different things, and for a long time I thought I wanted the thing a faculty position gives you.

What a faculty job offers is independence and time. You pick your problems, you train students, and you get to think on a ten-year horizon. I'd spent years preparing for that, and there's a real pull to it. Nobody tells you what to work on.

But the question I kept coming back to was: what is the bottleneck for the thing I actually care about? For robot learning, I became convinced the bottleneck isn't ideas. There are plenty of good ideas. The bottleneck is data, hardware at scale, and the ability to run the full loop fast, from collecting demonstrations to training a large model to deploying it on real robots and seeing what breaks. In an academic lab you can do a slice of that, and you can do it very well, but you're usually working with a handful of arms and a few students, and a lot of your energy goes into writing grants to keep that going.

At Physical Intelligence, that loop is the whole company. I could be in a room with people who had already shown that scaling works in language, and were betting the same recipe could work for physical action. That's a hypothesis you can only really test with a certain amount of compute and a certain amount of robot time, and it felt like the window for testing it was now, not in five years once a lab was built up.

The other thing was the people. I'd worked with some of them before, and the density of talent was unusual. In academia you build a group over time; here it was already there.

What I gave up is real. I don't have students in the same way, and the research agenda is shared rather than mine. But I told myself that if the goal is to actually make general-purpose robots work, I should be where the probability of that happening is highest, and that was the deciding factor.

For me, it came down to where I could do the research I cared about most. A faculty position was very appealing—the freedom to build a research agenda, work with students, and think long term. So it was a real tradeoff.

But with robotics, there’s also the question of what you can accomplish with a team working closely together, sharing infrastructure and pushing toward the same goal. Physical Intelligence felt like an opportunity to make that kind of concentrated effort. I ultimately leaned toward being part of that team and seeing how far we could take it.

For me, it came down to the kind of environment where I could do the work I wanted to do. A faculty position offers a lot of independence—you can build a group, mentor students, and pursue questions over a long period of time. That was very appealing.

But with Physical Intelligence, the opportunity was to work closely with a team focused on a shared problem, with the engineering and experimental effort that robotics requires. I felt that could let me move faster and learn a lot. It was a difficult choice, but ultimately I was more excited about that day-to-day experience.
